Reproductive investment in the white sea catfish Genidens barbus has been quantified through several key metrics derived from field-sampled adults in the Patos Lagoon estuary. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 10% [GSI = 10%] under the prevailing thermal regime of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C] during the spawning season. Males of this species are mouthbrooders, carrying fertilised eggs and early yolk-sac larvae within the buccal cavity until the onset of exogenous feeding, a costly parental investment that may constrain the relative mass of gonadal tissue that can be developed prior to spawning. The data were collected through routine gillnet surveys and subsequent laboratory dissection of reproductively active individuals. The temperature of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C] during the reproductive period aligns with the optimal thermal window for embryonic development in this subtropical population, where warmer waters accelerate yolk consumption and shorten the brooding interval.

Age and size at the onset of sexual maturity in Genidens barbus have been determined from macroscopic and histological examination of gonadal development across a large sample of individuals from southern Brazil. The total length at puberty, defined as the size at which fifty percent of the population exhibits actively gametogenic gonads, is 41.5 cm [Lp = 41.5 cm]. Concurrently, the wet weight at puberty for a fish of this length, derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship, is 647 grams [Wwp = 647 grams]. These benchmarks indicate that the species delays reproductive activity until it has attained a substantial body size, a pattern common among long-lived estuarine predators that require several years of somatic growth before allocating energy to gamete production. The length-weight allometry used for these calculations was validated against freshly weighed and measured specimens during the same sampling campaigns, ensuring reliable estimates of mass at maturation. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that a puberty length of 41.5 cm represents a relatively late maturation threshold within the Ariidae, likely linked to the energetic demands of oral incubation, which requires a sufficiently large buccal cavity and robust body condition to carry developing embryos through the brooding period without compromising the parent's own feeding efficiency.

The ultimate or asymptotic size of Genidens barbus provides a framework for understanding its lifetime growth trajectory and maximum reproductive potential. Based on extensive field measurements of the largest individuals captured over a multi-year monitoring program, the ultimate total length reaches 120 cm [Li = 120 cm]. Converting this asymptotic length into mass using the validated length-weight equation yields an ultimate wet weight of approximately 16,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 16,700 grams], a figure that places the white sea catfish among the larger-bodied members of its genus. This substantial adult mass is associated with a predatory, benthic-feeding ecology that exploits abundant crustacean and fish prey in coastal and estuarine systems. The slow attainment of such a large adult size is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises somatic persistence and reproductive longevity over rapid, early maturation, a pattern reinforced by the species' extended lifespan. Individuals exceeding 100 cm in total length are encountered infrequently but regularly in deeper channels of the Patos Lagoon, where they occupy the apex of the benthic food web and exhibit low natural mortality, consistent with the predictions of life-history theory for large-bodied, late-maturing marine teleosts.

The early life stages of Genidens barbus begin with relatively large, yolk-rich eggs that support an extended period of endogenous nutrition before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth, determined from the diameter of newly spawned ova measuring approximately 13 mm, is calculated as 1.15 grams [Wwb = 1.15 grams] using the geometric formula for a sphere and an assumed tissue density near unity. This substantial birth mass, which is unusually high among teleost fishes, reflects the large egg size typical of ariid catfishes and underpins the production of well-developed, yolk-sac larvae at the moment of hatching. The yolk reserves sustain the prolarvae through the initial days of development within the male's buccal cavity, where they remain protected from predation and environmental stressors until their mouth gapes open and they begin to capture small zooplankton. Field observations indicate that this oral incubation period lasts for several weeks, during which the larvae depend entirely on their endogenous yolk stores. The transition to exogenous feeding marks a critical bottleneck in early survival, as larvae must successfully capture adequate zooplankton prey while avoiding predation in the shallow nursery habitats of the estuarine margins.

Lifespan and reproductive scheduling in Genidens barbus are shaped by the relatively stable thermal conditions of its subtropical estuarine habitat. The maximum longevity recorded for this species, based on otolith increment analysis of the oldest individuals sampled, is approximately 36 years [am = approximately 36 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, nearing four decades, places the white sea catfish among the more long-lived members of the marine catfish assemblage along the southwestern Atlantic coastline, a trait that likely buffers the population against sporadic recruitment failures. The combination of a large ultimate size, a delayed puberty, and a long maximum age implies a low natural mortality rate and a conservative life-history strategy in which reproductive value accumulates slowly over many years. Such longevity also necessitates consistent, multi-decadal monitoring to understand the population dynamics and ensure sustainable management of this commercially important species. The otolith-derived age estimates have been cross-validated with length-frequency analysis, confirming that individuals up to 120 cm in total length correspond to the oldest age classes, reinforcing the link between asymptotic size and maximum longevity in this slow-growing ariid catfish.
